data.text:
F21 is fixed at records 99 and 100 and verified independently of the implementer that
wrote it. Six probes as `service_role` and then as the owner, in one rolled-back
transaction, against a freshly reset database:

| What was tried | Result |
|---|---|
| Erase the tenant, which is deletion on request | succeeded, audit events 2 to 0 |
| Re-create the same tenant id | refused 23001 |
| Create a brand new tenant | accepted |
| `service_role` reads the registry | refused 42501 |
| Owner deletes the tombstone | refused 23001 |
| Owner re-creates the erased id | refused 23001 |

The first row is the one worth naming, because it is the half a careless fix would have
broken. The exception in the append-only trigger is not an oversight: the PRD promises
deletion on request within 30 days, and an audit table nothing can delete from cannot
keep that promise. So the fix had to leave the erasure working and take away only the
reuse of the id. It does: the audit events still go with the tenant, and the third row
shows a fresh tenant is still creatable, so nothing legitimate was closed off.

The tombstone holds two columns, `tenant_id` and `erased_at`, confirmed from
`pg_attribute`. No name, no user, no buyer data. It records that an erasure happened and
not who was erased, which is why keeping it is not a retained record of an erased
customer, and it sits in `seen` because the Data API does not expose that schema and a
registry of erasures is not tenant-scoped data.

The registry's own append-only rule was written with no exception branch and no
subquery, deliberately, so that it does not repeat the shape of F23 in the very round
that was told to leave F23 alone.

Three limits, stated rather than left to be found:

- A restored dump taken before an erasure brings the id back with no tombstone. That is
  named in the migration's own account of what the guarantee is not, and it belongs to
  SEEN-082's restore drill.
- `revoke all on seen.erased_tenants` does not bind future tables in schema `seen`. That
  schema has no `pg_default_acl` entry today so a new table there starts owner-only, but
  part 6 narrowed the default privileges of `public` only. An `alter default privileges
  in schema seen` added later would make the next `seen` table born reachable and nothing
  asserts against it. This is the `seen`-side twin of the hazard part 6 closed.
- The owner can still drop or disable the triggers, set `session_replication_role` to
  `replica`, or drop the registry. Nothing is claimed about the WAL, a backup or a
  restore. That is the same boundary part 2 already draws for `audit_events`.

One piece of test hygiene found and not fixed: the tests that seed and erase tenants
outside a transaction now leave permanent tombstones in the local database, so the
registry grows across runs until the next `pnpm db:reset`. No test reuses an id, so
nothing fails today.

F23 is untouched, as this round was told. It still lives in `seen.refuse_audit_mutation`,
which is invoker-rights, so its `not exists` over `public.tenants` still tests visibility
rather than existence. F22 is also untouched. Both remain open.
